rationale: Evidence from iteration 5: widening the sensor span to x = ±0.06 cut line-loss events sharply on the s-bend (1.00 to 0.25) and slalom (1.05 to 0.85), and oval losses fell to 0.0. But the score fell from 238.1 to 219.9. Oval finishes dropped from 8 to 7 of 20, mean oval score fell from 567 to 492, and s-bend and slalom still end off track in every run. Completion bonuses dominate the score, so the wider span cost more on oval completion than it gained on losses. The Evaluator's rule is to revert the span when the score falls below 238, so I revert to x = ±0.04 (sensor positions -0.04, -0.02, 0, 0.02, 0.04). The span result is still a useful signal: fewer line losses suggest sensing contributes to the failures. To test the next suspect while keeping the span, I change sensor_size from 0.012 to 0.016 (16 mm footprint). Larger footprints should see the 25 mm tape earlier at the sharpest bends. Everything else is held at the iteration 4 values: kd 0.55, kp 4.0, ki 0.2, base_speed 1.5, weights (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2), last_direction, and the same body, wheel and sensor-y geometry. So any race difference is attributable to sensor_size. Expected result: line_loss_events on s-bend and slalom fall below 1.0 while oval finishes stay at or above 8 of 20 and the score holds near or above 238. Risks: a larger footprint averages more background and may blunt the signal at the centre, which could raise rms_error or steering_oscillation. If the score falls below 238 or steering_oscillation exceeds about 0.32, revert sensor_size to 0.012 and keep the iteration 4 design. Hypotheses: (a) line losses at the sharpest bends come from sensors that are too small to see the tape there; (b) the wider span hurt oval finishes because the outer sensors see the tape too late on tight oval curves. Measurements wanted: line_loss_events, max_error, steering_oscillation and rms_error per track, plus completion and completion_time on the oval.
